title: Front-end development
description: Review the code that runs in the browser or the app: rendering, state, accessibility in code, performance and browser support.
questions: Where does the interface render, and how does it load and update its state?
Which browsers, devices and assistive technologies must it support?
What does the change add to what users download and to the time before they can interact?

specialists.title: Rendering and state engineer
specialists.focus: Check where each view renders, server or client, how data is fetched and cached, and that loading, empty and error states exist.
checks: Each data-driven view has loading, empty, error and partial states.
Server state and local UI state are kept apart, and cache invalidation after a write is defined.
Hydration or client navigation does not show content that differs from the server render.

specialists.title: Semantic markup and accessibility engineer
specialists.focus: Check that components use native HTML elements and roles, have accessible names and manage focus as WCAG 2.2 requires.
checks: Buttons and links are native elements, not clickable divs.
Every input has a programmatic label and errors are announced.
Focus moves to opened dialogs, returns on close and is never hidden behind sticky content (WCAG 2.2 criterion 2.4.11).

specialists.title: Front-end performance engineer
specialists.focus: Measure what the change adds to the JavaScript, CSS and images users download and its effect on Core Web Vitals at the 75th percentile.
checks: The bundle size difference of the change is measured and compared with the budget.
LCP stays at or under 2.5 s, INP at or under 200 ms and CLS at or under 0.1 for the affected pages at p75.
Images have dimensions set and are lazy-loaded below the fold.

specialists.title: Browser and device support engineer
specialists.focus: Check the change against the project's supported browsers and devices, and plan a fallback for platform features that are not available everywhere.
checks: The supported browser list is written down and the features used are available in all of them, or have a fallback.
The change is tested on the smallest supported screen and with touch input.
Errors in the browser are reported to monitoring with the release version.

evidence: Component code and stories or screenshots of each state of the changed views.
Bundle size report and Core Web Vitals field or lab data before and after the change.
Accessibility check results: keyboard path, screen reader announcements and automated scan.
Supported browser and device list and the test results on them.
challenge: What does a user on a slow phone and network see during the first three seconds?
Could the same result use an existing component instead of a new one?
Which state, such as an expired session or a failed save, has no designed screen?
Does a new dependency justify its weight compared with a few lines of code?
decision_criteria: Proceed when every state renders, the accessibility checks pass and the performance budget holds on the affected pages.
Revise when the change breaks keyboard use, exceeds the bundle budget or fails on a supported browser.
Ask for a feature flag or staged rollout when the change alters navigation or rendering for all pages.
Name the front-end metric, such as p75 INP or JavaScript error rate, and its threshold after release.
